paras: The lynching of Laura Porter was the seizure of a Black woman from the city jail of Monroe, Louisiana, in late July 1910 by unidentified men, who were believed to have drowned her in the Ouachita River. No trace of her was reported found, and a Louisiana weekly described the affair as "what appears to have been a lynching." A South Carolina paper ran the news under the headline "Shame on Louisiana."

Porter was in jail after an arrest for larceny, and the Black-press brief said she had been warned many times to leave town beforehand. She was described as the keeper of a "resort" where several white men were reported to have been robbed. Le Meschacébé called her "a notorious dive-keeper" whose most frequent offense was robbing white men, charging that she had two or three Black male confederates.

According to a Monroe dispatch datelined July 27, men whose identity the police could not establish broke into the jail and carried her off. Le Meschacébé reported that a party of masked men took her "quietly" about midnight, so the seizure may have occurred on the night of July 26-27. Other women prisoners said she was taken out nude and that the men returned an hour later for her clothing. The common belief was that she was thrown into the Ouachita River and drowned, according to the Louisiana paper with iron weights tied to her.
No body, inquest or arrest is reported in the coverage, and Le Meschacébé wrote that what happened to her "may never be known."

The earliest report found ran on August 3 in the Edgefield Advertiser of South Carolina, which printed the Monroe special twice under the headline "Shame on Louisiana"; the Dillon Herald reprinted it on August 18. In Louisiana, Le Meschacébé headlined the story "Divekeeper May Be Drowned" with the subhead "Indignant Citizens Believed to Have Thrown Woman Into River," and devoted much of its account to her record with the police.

The Black press coverage found consists of a single brief in the Colorado Statesman on August 6, printed without comment in its "Race News" column alongside a New York real estate sale and a Philadelphia obituary. That version was the only one to mention her arrest for larceny and the repeated warnings to leave town.

reader.title: Lynching of Laura Porter
bases: Men broke into the Monroe city jail, took out a Black woman prisoner, and were believed to have drowned her in the Ouachita River; Le Meschacébé called it 'what appears to have been a lynching' (A1, A3, A4).

Men with no lawful authority seized Porter from jail over accusations of robbing white men, but her death was only 'believed' and no body was reported found, and the party's size is not given beyond 'men' and 'a party of masked men' (A1, A3, A4).

A Monroe special in the white press, a Black-press news brief, and a fuller Louisiana account agree that men took Porter from the jail and that she was believed drowned in the Ouachita, though none reports a body (A1, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Monroe special (wire)
accounts.gist: Unidentified men broke into the jail and carried off Porter, at whose home white men were reported robbed; she was generally believed thrown into the Ouachita and drowned. The Black-press version adds her arrest for larceny after repeated warnings to leave town.

accounts.label: Le Meschacébé (Louisiana paper)
accounts.gist: A party of masked men quietly took her from the city jail about midnight; women prisoners said she was taken out nude and the men came back an hour later for her clothes; the belief was she was drowned with iron weights tied to her.

framing.detail: The Edgefield Advertiser ran the Monroe special under the headline 'Shame on Louisiana', reprinted by the Dillon Herald.

Le Meschacébé called it 'what appears to have been a lynching' but headlined the captors 'Indignant Citizens' and dwelt on Porter as a 'notorious dive-keeper' who gave police more trouble than the rest of the tenderloin.
The Colorado Statesman printed the wire item without comment in its 'Race News' column, between a real estate sale and an obituary.
